summary: This benchmark evaluates affine bridge maps between Qwen2.5-14B host activations and the final FFN layer of Qwen2.5-Coder-7B on a bracket-matching task. The study shows that calibrating on matched synthetic Python prompts restores the matching-bracket log-odds signal to +2.040, closely matching the native donor baseline (+2.049) and substantially outperforming an archived map calibrated on generic code. The benchmark is methodologically rigorous and reproducible, though focused on a narrow syntactic probe.
strengths: Rigorous experimental controls that isolate destination bias by measuring pairwise log-odds differences between symmetric opening bracket variants.
Comprehensive statistical reporting with paired 95% bootstrap confidence intervals for both log-odds effects and task completion counts.
Clear specification of baselines including native donor upper bound, zero-module ablation, and the previous generic calibration map.
Precise documentation of model commit hashes, layer cut points, linear algebra formulations, and software dependency versions.
weaknesses: The evaluation is restricted to a narrow syntactic probe (bracket closure over 256 synthetic groups) rather than comprehensive code generation benchmarks like HumanEval or MBPP.
Experiments are limited to a single donor-host architecture pair (Qwen2.5-14B and Qwen2.5-Coder-7B), leaving cross-family generalization unaddressed.
Focuses strictly on the input mapping interface; end-to-end generative coherence after routing back into host downstream layers remains unmeasured.
suggestions: Extend the benchmarking suite to broader semantic code completion tasks to test whether affine feature alignment preserves complex contextual dependencies.
Evaluate cross-architecture pairings (e.g., Llama-3 to Qwen) to test the limits of affine activation alignment across disparate tokenizers and latent spaces.
Benchmark full round-trip inference where the transformed expert outputs are integrated into subsequent host transformer layers.
